key_gap: Both sides selected the same constraint-derived design (monolith + Postgres with batched upserts for locations, transactions on assignment state, in-memory write-through cache for the dispatcher; rejected Kafka/event-sourcing/CQRS), but the human derived it at first sight: it enumerated constraints in fixed order (data, scale, latency, failure modes, change rate), ran the loss-consequence test on each data flow ('what happens if this write is lost? duplicated?') and got the non-obvious read — location pings are ephemeral sensor readings, not events; assignment state is the system of record, not the event log — then derived module boundaries from change rate (frozen pipeline vs weekly rules). The AI opened with the team's pattern as the working hypothesis and needed a full WHY falsification pass (throughput math vs 20k+ tps, async-hop latency analysis) to reach the same design, spending a stage it did not need.
learning_signal: For architecture decisions, classify data by loss-consequence before comparing patterns: for each data flow ask 'what happens if this write is lost? duplicated? delayed?' — loss-invisible data (sensor readings, logs) is ephemeral and wants cheap batched writes with no recovery ceremony; loss-visible data (assignments, orders, money) is durable and wants transactions and single-owner writes. Run scale and latency as arithmetic (peak rate vs capacity; the async-hop cost against the freshness bound) so non-constraints are identified before pattern selection — throughput below ~10–20k writes/s generally makes queue/stream infrastructure a solution in search of a problem — and draw module boundaries from change rate (frozen pipeline vs weekly-changing rules), which CQRS-style projection coupling violates.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'constraint pre-screen' to WHAT for architecture/design tasks, run before any alternative is generated: (a) enumerate the data flows and classify each by loss-consequence (ephemeral vs durable) with the stated consequence of loss/duplication; (b) compute steady and peak rates and compare against a one-instance RDBMS baseline to flag non-binding scale; (c) state the freshness/latency bound and check every proposed hop against it; (d) split modules by change rate. Treat a proposed pattern name as a hypothesis to be tested against these, not a default — when the proposal arrives, the loss-consequence taxonomy should be the first frame, not the falsification target.

key_gap: The pure style approved a derived S3-log ledger (append-only log + in-memory balance cache + idempotency keys + hourly reconciliation) as the system of record for money movement, dismissing the SQL double-entry transactional ledger as cargo-cult. The derivation was valid within an incomplete constraint list: throughput was enumerated (and is a non-constraint at 12–200/s vs 10k+ tps RDBMS), while the binding constraints — crash atomicity at the mutation boundary and an auditable single source of truth per mutation — were never named. The AI modeled the crash window (between log append and cache apply, divergence has no transaction boundary to attribute it to; reconciliation detects but cannot classify it, and repair cost grows multiplicatively with partitions), found the repair unbounded, checked the scale arithmetic, and retained the battle-tested transactional ledger (partition by account) with the derived log demoted to an archive tier.
learning_signal: A first-principles derivation is only as good as its constraint list: when the failure-mode enumeration is self-generated and not checked against the ecosystem's, binding constraints get omitted and the design optimizes the enumerated non-constraint. Two completeness tests: (1) the crash-window test — for every derived multi-step write path, ask 'what is the state when a process dies between step N and N+1, and how is it attributed and repaired?' — a design whose repair is detection-without-attribution (reconciliation that cannot classify divergence) is not eventually consistent, it is unrepairable; (2) the pattern-encoding question — when rejecting a battle-tested pattern, ask 'what failure mode does this pattern encode, and have I enumerated it?' SQL transactions encode exactly the crash-atomicity and single-source-of-truth constraints the naive derivation omitted. Where the pattern exists and the domain is high-stakes (money, safety), the burden of proof is on the derivation, not on the pattern.
suggested_improvement: Add an 'ecosystem benchmark pass' to HOW, mandatory for any derived design that rejects a standard pattern: (a) name the constraint the pattern encodes (for a transactional ledger: crash atomicity at the mutation boundary, auditable per-mutation single truth); (b) run the crash-window test on the derived design's write path (state between steps, attribution, repair cost as a function of partitions); (c) verify the enumerated constraints are actually binding with arithmetic (throughput vs capacity) before optimizing them; (d) either adopt the pattern or document a residual-risk trade the derivation accepted. This converts the AI's correct-but-late catch (the WHY falsification stage did the work) into a first-pass check.
